source.title: Encourage or Inhibit Monosemanticity? Revisit Monosemanticity from a Feature Decorrelation Perspective
source.authors: Hanqi Yan; Yanzheng Xiang; Guang-Yi Chen; Yifei Wang; Lin Gui; Yu-Lan He

page_placements.theme: Scale and fine-tuning trends in neuron monosemanticity proxies

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures monosemanticity using proxies rather than auditing the share of neuron poles with one or two jobs. Its cross-model comparisons bear conceptually on whether monosemanticity is similar across model sizes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no percentage of neuron poles with one or two jobs. The Pythia comparisons discussed in the text are cited from Gurnee et al. (2023), not results from this study, so they are not rows. Figures 2–4 also report proxy changes after DPO; those results concern a training effect not covered by the listed versions and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study never audits what share of neurons have one, two or unclear jobs. It measures proxies: the weight-norm times bias product from Gurnee et al., and activation decorrelation. These are a related but different construct from the per-neuron job counts that V1 and V2 name, so no version is tested. Its cross-model proxy comparison and its DPO effects go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that DPO raises monosemanticity proxies, that there is no clear relation between monosemanticity and model size, and that monosemanticity should be encouraged. Their decorrelation regularizer (DecPO) raises decorrelation, activation sparsity and alignment scores. Their stated limitations are ad hoc analysis, Llama-family models only with limited data, and Llama3-8b as the largest model studied.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation-correlation and weight/bias-product proxies for monosemanticity rather than a pole-by-pole audit with explanations tested on held-out activations; also studies DPO and decorrelation regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different proxy behavior across relative layer depth: DPO improves the proxy in earlier layers but the proxy declines in later layers. It also reports feature-decorrelation measurements by dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: The weight-norm times bias proxy for monosemanticity shows no consistent ordering by size across GPT-2 medium/large/xl, GPT-neo-2.7B and GPT-J-6B. The authors say comparing different models may be unreliable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Proxy-measured monosemanticity (Gurnee weight-bias product) does not vary consistently with model size across GPT-style models.

fits_no_version.finding: After DPO the weight-bias proxy rises in earlier layers of the GPT-2 models and falls in later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DPO raises a weight-based monosemanticity proxy in earlier layers but lowers it in later layers.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO increases activation decorrelation in Llama-2-7b-hf on the Wiki, Cog and Syco datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DPO increases MLP activation decorrelation, a proxy for monosemanticity.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study uses proxies rather than direct neuron-pole explanations and reports no percentages of poles by job count. Figure 2 provides no numerical model-level share values. Its authors note that their analysis is ad hoc, models are limited to the Llama family and limited data in the alignment experiments, and the largest alignment model is Llama3-8b.
record.rows_left_out: No additional V2 rows were left out. Other reported regularizer and preference-alignment results do not measure the cross-model neuron-pole shares named by the listed versions.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit of neuron poles by number of jobs.
No audit of the share of neurons with one or two jobs in any model; GPT-2, GPT-neo and GPT-J get only proxy curves; no mixture-of-experts or trillion-parameter models.
No InceptionV1 or cat-and-car neuron analysis.
No comparison of interpretable-neuron shares across architectures or tools.
No test of explanations against held-out activations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked r1–r5 to V2 and labelled them limits_scope. That is removed: the proxy is a different construct from the share of neurons with one job. Table 1 (top tokens per layer after DecPO) is a qualitative interpretability illustration with no share, so it is not recorded as missing. The Pythia comparisons in the text are cited from Gurnee et al. and are correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or estimates of the shares of poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
The study compares proxies across GPT-2-family/GPT-style models only; it does not audit shares, test mixture-of-experts models, or study models up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or pose/recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of interpretability shares across architectures or tools, and no estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
No attribution-graph reconstruction or comparison with a trained replacement model.
No test of explanations against new activating examples or prediction of where neurons fire.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: Discusses neuron monosemanticity and polysemanticity through proxies and a regularizer, with no audit of how many neurons have one job.

tranche.reason: Measures proxies only: the weight-norm x bias product (from Gurnee et al.) and activation decorrelation. This is a related but different construct from the per-neuron job shares in V1/V2, so the study neither tests nor uses any version.

source_check.notes: Proxy-only study: weight-norm x bias product on GPT-2, GPT-neo and GPT-J, and activation decorrelation on Llama. The authors say comparisons across model families may not be reliable. The Figure 3 legend also lists GPT-neo(2.7B), but the text says DPO was run on three GPT-2 variants. The Llama DecPO/decorrelation results are not among the 8 rows checked.

statements.problem: None. Figure 2 plots all five models, and its caption says there is no consistent correlation with model size. The written comparison covers GPT-2 medium/large/xl and GPT-neo, and the DPO run was on GPT-2 models only. The statement matches both.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GPT-2/GPT-style models shown in Figure 2, from 355M to 6B
reader_labels.reason: The authors report no clear relationship between proxy monosemanticity and model size, and say cross-model comparisons may be unreliable; these measurements do not establish similar neuron-pole shares. See r1–r5.
